div.head: About the Edition
div.p: Probstücke Digital is a digital edition of the 24 Prob-Stücke (test pieces) that form the “Ober-Classe” of Johann Mattheson’s thoroughbass treatise. Each Prob-Stück is a figured bass, one in each of the 24 keys, followed by Mattheson’s Erläuterung: a commentary that discusses individual bars and often shows in a short music example how the right hand might be realised.

Mattheson published the treatise twice: as Exemplarische Organisten-Probe im Artikel vom General-Bass (Hamburg: Schiller und Kißner, 1719) and, revised and enlarged, as Grosse General-Baß-Schule (Hamburg: Kißner, 1731). The edition presents both versions, so that Mattheson’s revisions of the music and of the commentary can be followed piece by piece.

list.item: The figured basses of all 24 Prob-Stücke, encoded in MEI. One encoding per piece records both prints. Where they differ, both readings are encoded, and each page shows the reading of the print it belongs to. Modern clefs, key signatures and accidentals are encoded as editorial alternatives to the printed ones, so that the music can be shown in the original or in modern notation.
Diplomatic transcriptions of Mattheson’s commentary from both prints, encoded in TEI: all 24 from 1719 and all 24 from 1731.
An English translation of the commentary by Niels Pfeffer, made from the 1731 text.

Lessons and realisations: two lessons that Robert Hill gave on Probstücke 3 and 4 at the Hochschule für Musik Freiburg in May 2019 and one on Probstück 16 in June 2019, transcribed from audio recordings; a realisation of Probstück 4 by Dijoux with notes in French, also in English translation; realisations of Probstücke 10 and 14 by Niels Pfeffer and of Probstücke 20 and 21 by Larry Molinaro, with recordings.
Editorial notes, and indices of the persons, literature and musical works mentioned in the commentary, linked to the Integrated Authority File (GND) where possible.

An index of terms based on Mattheson’s own Register of the 1731 print: every subject entry that refers to the Ober-Classe, with a modern German form, an English gloss and links to the passages; the editors have added some references Mattheson does not give. The Register itself is transcribed as well.

div.head: Printings and Copies
div.p: The 1731 treatise was printed twice. The edition follows the first printing: its title page, in red and black, is dated 1731, and it has 484 pages, the last of them a list of misprints. A later printing, without a date on its black title page, was set anew from the first: it has 460 pages, the misprints are corrected and the spelling is modernised. This edition follows the earlier printing. A digital copy of the later printing is available from the Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Hamburg (MS 163/2b).

div.head: Selection
div.p: Both versions of the treatise consist of a theoretical preparation, 24 easier examples and the 24 more difficult Prob-Stücke. The edition covers the Prob-Stücke with their commentaries. The preparation and the easier examples are not included.

div.head: Editorial Approach
div.p: Music and text are encoded following the standards of the Music Encoding Initiative (MEI) and the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI). The commentary is transcribed diplomatically following the Base Format of the Deutsches Textarchiv (DTABf), preserving original spelling, line beginnings, catchwords and page breaks. The rules are described in the editorial guidelines.

For easier reading, the website shows the 1719 and 1731 commentaries in modernised spelling. The modern forms come from a word list kept with the data (normalisation/lexicon.tsv); words not listed only get the long s and the umlauts in modern form. Names and foreign words keep their spelling. The word list was started from the normalisation service CAB of the Deutsches Textarchiv and is being reviewed; not every entry has been checked yet. Point at a word to see its original spelling. The diplomatic view (the switch Modern / Diplomatic / Facsimile at the top of the page) shows the commentary as printed instead, with the long s, the umlauts and the spelling of the print, and marks the end of each of its lines with a vertical stroke, as critical editions do (“gerne | mit”, within a word “ſchwar-|tzen”); there, point at a word to see its modern form. The diplomatic transcription itself is contained in the TEI files, which can be downloaded from every page.

div.head: Reading the Edition
div.p: On each page the score is on the left and the commentary on the right. Highlighted passages in the commentary refer to bars, notes or figures in the score: point at a passage to see them marked in the score, or at a marked element in the score to find the passage. Point at a line of music to see it in the original print. On a touch screen, tap instead of pointing, and tap a selected line of music again to see the print. The buttons above the score show or hide the upper staff with the right-hand passages notated in the print, and add or remove empty staves for writing out a realisation.

The switch Modern / Diplomatic / Facsimile at the top of the page applies to the text and the music alike: in modern spelling with modern clefs and accidentals, as printed, with the original clefs and accidentals, or in the page images of the print. The website remembers the choice for all pages.

The facsimile shows the score page by page on the left, as large as the screen allows, and the pages of the commentary on the right. Where the paragraphs of the commentary and the bars of the score are marked on the pages (so far in the 1731 print of Probstücke 1 to 21), the bars that the commentary refers to are tinted: point at a paragraph to see the bars it refers to (the score turns to their page; the numbers of the pages with such bars are underlined), or at a bar to see the paragraphs about it; click a bar to bring the first of them into view. On a touch screen, tap instead of pointing. Where there are no page images yet, the transcription is shown as printed.

The commentary can be compared sentence by sentence: beneath each sentence of the English translation stands, small and grey, the sentence of the 1731 text it translates; beneath each sentence of one print, the corresponding sentence of the other, so that Mattheson’s revisions of 1731 can be followed. Sentences that he added or left out have nothing beneath them. The button with the subtitles icon at the top of the page hides or shows these lines.
